record.paper_title: Massive Stars: Some Open Questions and the role of Multi-Object Spectroscopy
record.original_question: Why do evolutionary masses and spectroscopic masses of massive stars still disagree, and what physical or modeling ingredients are needed to remove the remaining mass discrepancy? The unresolved issue is that masses inferred by placing stars in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and comparing with evolutionary tracks are still systematically inconsistent with masses inferred from stellar-atmosphere analyses of spectra, even after improvements such as line blanketing in atmosphere models and rotational mixing in evolutionary models. Current discrepancies are smaller than in the original reports, but they still persist at the level of about 20% to 50% across the Milky Way, the Large Magellanic Cloud, and the Small Magellanic Cloud.

evidence.quote: Although both techniques should give the comsistent masses, Herrero et al. (1992) showed that there is a systematic discrepancy between both (the mass discrepancy).

There have even been claims that the problem was solved thanks to these improvements (Weidner & Vink 2010), at least within errors. However, the literature is plaged with examples of the mass discrepancy.
Thus we may conclude that the mass discrepancy is still controversial and remains as a problem, but at a milder scale (20-50%) than when it was first detected.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a massive star (initial mass ≳ 10 M☉), two independent methods are used to estimate its current mass:

1. The evolutionary mass M_evol, obtained by placing the star at its measured effective temperature and luminosity on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram and reading off the mass from a grid of stellar evolutionary tracks (which may include rotational mixing, overshooting, and prescribed mass loss).

2. The spectroscopic mass M_spec, obtained from a quantitative non-LTE stellar-atmosphere analysis of the star's spectrum, which yields the surface gravity log g and effective temperature T_eff; together with the radius R inferred from luminosity and T_eff, this gives M_spec = g R² / G.

Empirically, in samples of OB stars in the Milky Way, the Large Magellanic Cloud, and the Small Magellanic Cloud, these two estimates disagree systematically: even after incorporating line blanketing in the atmosphere models and rotational mixing in the evolutionary models, residual differences |M_evol − M_spec| / M_evol of order 20%–50% persist, generally in the sense that M_evol > M_spec (the "mass discrepancy").

Problem. Identify the physical or modeling ingredient(s) — for instance, prescriptions for mass loss, internal mixing, convective core boundary treatment, binarity and mass transfer, magnetic fields, micro/macroturbulence in atmosphere modeling, treatment of the wind/photosphere transition, or other effects — whose inclusion (or correction) in the evolutionary tracks and/or in the atmosphere analyses is necessary and sufficient to bring M_evol and M_spec into statistical agreement across the Milky Way, LMC, and SMC samples. Equivalently, determine whether the residual 20%–50% discrepancy reflects a genuine deficiency of stellar evolution theory, of stellar atmosphere theory, of the observational inputs (T_eff, log g, L, distance), or some combination thereof.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature continues to report a residual systematic difference between evolutionary and spectroscopic masses of OB-type and red supergiant stars. A 2018 A&A study of Galactic O-type stars finds the mass discrepancy persists and varies with luminosity/mass regime; a 2024 study of red supergiants at subsolar metallicity proposes that intrinsically hotter temperatures (lower TiO opacity) can largely reconcile the masses for that subclass, but no single ingredient has been shown to remove the discrepancy uniformly across MW/LMC/SMC OB-star samples. The problem remains open, with partial progress in specific regimes.

status_evidence.title: Spectroscopic and physical parameters of Galactic O-type stars – III. Mass discrepancy and rotational mixing
status_evidence.snippet: Stars with log L/L☉≳5.65 and Minit≥40 M☉ appear over-massive by ~20%–70%; lower-luminosity stars show spectroscopic masses smaller than evolutionary masses by ~20–29%.
status_evidence.claim: The evolutionary–spectroscopic mass discrepancy persists in Galactic O stars with regime-dependent magnitude.

status_evidence.title: Investigating episodic mass loss in evolved massive stars II — RSGs at subsolar metallicity
status_evidence.snippet: RSGs are intrinsically hotter, decreasing TiO opacity and naturally resolving the discrepancy; the scaling relation should depend on metallicity and mass-loss rate.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress for red supergiants at low metallicity, but resolution depends on metallicity and mass-loss prescription.
